summary:
The project tackles the challenge through a decision support system that turns complex scientific data into simple information and concrete actions for farmers. Its simulations showed a potential 52% savings in irrigation water and a 70.9% reduction in forage losses during a drought scenario.

Little Farms 67 aims to strengthen the resilience of farms against climate change, reduce water waste, and bring Earth observation technologies closer to producers who need accessible tools to manage their resources.

In Patagonia, where water is a limited resource, making data-driven decisions can be the difference between losing a crop and saving it.
details:
Little Farms 67 is a web application that turns publicly available satellite and weather data into practical information for small-scale farmers.

Its goal is to help farmers:

Make efficient and responsible decisions about water use

Optimize irrigation and prepare for potentially catastrophic periods

The application works by integrating three main data sources:

N.A.S.A POWER: Provides daily data on temperature, precipitation, wind, and soil moisture.

N.A.S.A S.M.A.P: Provides information on surface and root-zone soil moisture.

Sentinel-2: Its products make it possible to monitor vegetation health through indices such as N.D.V.I.

Based on this data, and using F.A.Q-recognized methodologies, Little Farms 67:

Calculates crop water demand

Performs a daily soil water balance

Users can select their location, crop, and field area to view climate indicators, moisture trends, irrigation needs, and weekly recommendations. These are used to generate daily alerts with clear steps for the farmer to follow.

The platform also includes alerts for frost, high temperatures, dry spells, excessive rainfall, and other production risks detectable through NASA data. It also offers a virtual assistant with specialized answers, plus tools to estimate the economic benefits of more efficient water management.

The project was evaluated through two simulations on a 10-hectare demonstration alfalfa farm, using real NASA POWER weather records and different management scenarios. In the first, the system estimated a 52.2% saving in irrigation water compared with a traditional strategy. In the second, under a simulated scenario in which irrigation turns were cut by 80%, the early warning made it possible to apply a protocol that reduced forage losses from 18.2% to 5.3%. Both experiments were repeated 300 times with random variations to test how consistent the results were. These figures are simulation results and still need to be validated on real farms.

The main benefit of Little Farm is that it brings Earth observation and environmental analysis tools to farmers who usually lack the technical resources to interpret large volumes of data. Its expected impact is to reduce water waste, protect agricultural production, improve irrigation planning, and strengthen the resilience of rural farms against climate change and growing water uncertainty.

The project’s creativity lies in combining different scientific data sources into a simple, localized, decision-oriented tool. Instead of just showing maps or statistics, Little Farms 67 turns complex information into clear recommendations and action protocols for farmers, whether or not they have experience interpreting and using satellite data.

During development, the team took into account the specific conditions of Patagonia: low rainfall, high water demand in summer, reliance on canal irrigation systems, and possible restrictions on water delivery turns. It also considered affordability, ease of use, the availability of open data, the differences in resolution between satellite products, and the limitations of the models used.

Tools and technologies: Development is based on the N.A.S.A P.O.W.E.R Daily API, the S.M.A.P. and Sentinel-2 satellite products, FAO-56 water balance models, the Hargreaves–Samani evapotranspiration equation, and the F.A.Q-33 yield response model. The application pulls N.A.S.A POWER data directly from the browser and keeps a backup copy of the records used in the simulations.

Future Outlook

The next step for Little Farm is to validate its simulation results on real farms. The team plans to run pilot programs with farmers and cooperatives in Patagonia and compare the system’s recommendations with traditional irrigation practices. Low-cost soil moisture sensors will be used to calibrate the models against SMAP data and the FAO-56 water balance.

Once validated, the platform aims to:

Expand beyond alfalfa to fruit trees, grapevines, vegetables, and pastures

Reach other arid and semi-arid regions of Argentina and Latin America

Offer a mobile version with offline mode and alerts via WhatsApp or SMS

Add new satellite sources such as Landsat and ECOSTRESS to improve accuracy on small plots

In the long term, Little Farm could become a tool for collective water management. Irrigation districts, cooperatives, and public agencies could use it to plan irrigation turns, anticipate restrictions, and distribute water more fairly during scarce seasons.

The project’s sustainability rests on its tiered subscription model, complemented by partnerships with institutions such as INTA (Argentina’s National Agricultural Technology Institute), universities, and provincial governments to support validation, training, and access for small producers.

The vision of Little Farm is to make satellite information an everyday tool for any farmer, regardless of farm size or technical background, so that rural communities can use water more efficiently and be better prepared for an increasingly uncertain climate.
